name: sslsplit
desc: Man-in-the-middle attacks against SSL encrypted network connections
why: A transparent MITM proxy for SSL/TLS that makes the handshake and certificate trust model visible in a way few people have ever watched.

brief.what_it_is: SSLsplit is a transparent man-in-the-middle proxy for SSL/TLS connections. It takes in TCP connections that are redirected to it by a NAT engine (pf, ipfw, ipfilter, netfilter, or TPROXY, depending on OS), or connections to static or SNI-derived destinations. It terminates the client's TLS session using forged X.509 certificates it signs on the fly (or existing certificates whose keys you supply), opens a new TLS connection to the real server, and logs what passes through. Output is connect logs, content logs (per-connection files or a pipe), PCAP files, master key logs in SSLKEYLOGFILE format, and optionally decrypted traffic mirrored to a network interface. It also handles plain TCP upgraded to TLS for STARTTLS-style protocols.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says SSLsplit is 'intended to be useful for network forensics, application security analysis and penetration testing.' It is meant for examining what encrypted traffic actually contains by sitting in the middle of it.
brief.how_it_works: Redirected connections arrive at SSLsplit, which terminates TLS toward the client using a forged certificate that copies the original server's subject DN, subjectAltName and other characteristics, signed by a CA you provide with -c/-k. It then starts a fresh TLS connection to the original destination address (or a static or SNI-named host) and relays data in both directions while logging it. For HTTP(S), it rewrites headers to defeat HPKP, HSTS, Expect-CT and protocol upgrades, and disables compression and keep-alive so logs stay readable.

brief.install_notes: Available as a package on many systems, including Homebrew (sslsplit), Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, Arch, Kali, and FreeBSD ports. To build from source you need GNU make, a POSIX.2 environment, OpenSSL (or LibreSSL), libevent 2.x, libpcap and libnet 1.1.x; libpcap and libnet can be left out if you skip the mirroring feature. Dependencies are found through pkg-config; if that fails, set OPENSSL_BASE, LIBEVENT_BASE, LIBPCAP_BASE, LIBNET_BASE or CHECK_BASE. The README says SSL/TLS feature support depends heavily on the OpenSSL version linked. Beyond installing, you must set up a CA certificate and key for signing forged certs, configure a NAT rule on your platform to redirect traffic to SSLsplit, and manage privileges: run as root and it drops to user nobody by default (-u).
brief.standout: Most MITM demos hide the handshake behind a browser or a Python library. SSLsplit is a single C binary that sits on a real redirected network path and mints certificates live, so you can watch the trust model fail or hold. It also covers non-HTTP protocols: plain TCP or STARTTLS can be upgraded to TLS generically.
brief.status: Unknown for last commit. The homepage was dated 2025-02-04, its copyright runs to 2025, and it lists sslsplit-0.5.5 as the latest release, though no release date for 0.5.5 appears on the page. I did not check the GitHub repository for commit activity.
brief.caveats: It is a tool for intercepting traffic. The README gives no legal or consent guidance; use it only on networks and devices you are authorised to test. NAT support is limited to FreeBSD (pf, ipfw, ipfilter), OpenBSD (pf), Linux (netfilter REDIRECT and TPROXY) and macOS (ipfw, pf). Local process lookup (-i) works only on macOS and FreeBSD. It does not exploit certificate verification bugs in TLS stacks, though it does support NULL-prefix CN certificates. Protocol support spans SSL 3.0 through TLS 1.2, with SSL 2.0 optional, so modern TLS 1.3 is not mentioned in the README. The license is a two-clause BSD license.
quotes: SSLsplit is a tool for man-in-the-middle attacks against SSL/TLS encrypted network connections.
SSLsplit is purely a transparent proxy and cannot act as a HTTP or SOCKS proxy configured in a browser.
SSLsplit is designed to transparently terminate connections that are redirected to it using a network address translation engine.
